usage: 책상 좀 저쪽으로 옮겨 주세요.
Please move the desk over there.
옮기다 takes an object + a destination marked with -(으)로 ('toward'): 저쪽으로 옮기다.
다음 달에 회사를 옮겨요.
I'm changing companies next month.
Figurative job/seat change: 회사를 옮기다, 자리를 옮기다 — the 'relocate yourself to a new spot' sense.
감기를 옮기지 않게 마스크를 쓰세요.
Wear a mask so you don't pass on your cold.
옮기다 also means to transmit a disease: 감기를/병을 옮기다.
일정을 다음 주로 옮겼어요.
I moved the schedule to next week.
Abstract relocation in time: 일정을/날짜를 옮기다 = reschedule.
examples: 짐 좀 옮겨 주세요.
Please move the bags.
The bare polite request — 짐을 옮기다 is the textbook object + verb pair for luggage.
이사할 때 짐 옮기는 게 제일 힘들어요.
When you move house, hauling the stuff is the hardest part.
Note the division of labor: 이사하다 = move house (the whole event), 짐을 옮기다 = physically carry the boxes.
무거우니까 우리 같이 저 소파를 옮길까요?
It's heavy, so shall we move that sofa together?
Real-situation offer: 같이 + -(으)ㄹ까요? proposes doing the lifting as a team.
nuance: 옮기다 is the everyday transitive verb for relocating an object: you take hold of it and set it down in a new place, so it needs both an object (책상을) and usually a destination (저쪽으로). The sharpest contrast is with 움직이다, which means something stirs or budges where it is — 의자가 움직였어요 ('the chair shifted') versus 의자를 옮겼어요 ('I moved the chair to a new spot'). It also differs from 이사하다 (to move one's whole household) and from 나르다 (to ferry/haul loads back and forth, emphasizing the carrying labor). Koreans stretch 옮기다 figuratively to switching jobs (회사를 옮기다), seats (자리를 옮기다), schedules (일정을 옮기다), and even contagion (감기를 옮기다, 'pass on a cold'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using it intransitively like English 'move' in 'I'm moving next week' — for that you need 이사하다, because 옮기다 always demands the thing being moved.

mistakes: Don't say bare 옮겨요 for 'I'm moving (house)' — 옮기다 is transitive and needs an object; for relocating your home use 이사해요.
Don't confuse it with 움직이다: 움직이다 = something budges/stirs on its own (차가 움직여요), while 옮기다 = YOU carry an object to a new place (차를 옮겨요).
Don't drop the destination particle: it's 저쪽으로 옮기다 ('-(으)로' = toward), not '저쪽 옮기다'.

usage: 의자를 끌지 말고 들어서 옮기세요.
Don't drag the chair, lift it to move it.
끌다 = drag along a surface; contrasted here with 들다 (lift) because dragging scratches and screeches.
저 가게가 사람들의 관심을 끌어요.
That shop draws people's attention.
관심을 끌다 / 인기를 끌다 = attract attention/popularity — the most common figurative collocation.
캐리어를 끌고 공항에 갔어요.
I wheeled my suitcase to the airport.
끌고 가다 ('drag-and-go') is the set phrase for pulling wheeled luggage.
회의를 너무 끌지 마세요.
Don't drag the meeting out.
시간을/회의를 끌다 = stall, drag something out in time.
examples: 줄을 끌어요.
Pull the cord.
Bare command with 줄을 끌다 = pull a rope/leash/string toward you along the ground.
강아지가 산책할 때 자꾸 줄을 끌어요.
My puppy keeps tugging the leash on walks.
Everyday scene: 자꾸 ('keeps doing it') + 끌다 captures repeated tugging.
발표를 너무 오래 끌어서 사람들이 지루해했어요.
The presentation dragged on so long that people got bored.
Real-situation figurative use: 끌다 = drag out time, with the consequence (지루해하다) attached.
nuance: 끌다 covers two linked ideas: physically dragging something along a surface (a suitcase, a chair, a leash) and, figuratively, pulling something toward you — attention (관심을 끌다), popularity (인기를 끌다), or out in time (시간을 끌다). The near-synonym is 당기다, but the dividing line matters: 당기다 is a clean pull toward yourself in the air (문을 당기다 'pull the door'), while 끌다 implies dragging weight across the ground with friction. It is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ vanishes before consonant endings -ㅂ니다 and -(으)세요: 끕니다, 끄세요 — but it stays before vowels: 끌어요, 끌었어요. The dangerous trap for English speakers is the near-twin 끄다 ('to turn off', as in 불을 끄다); its imperative 꺼요/끄세요 sounds close to 끌다's forms, but they are entirely different verbs.

Don't use 끌다 for a crisp pull-toward-you with no friction (a door, a rope in the air) — that's 당기다; 끌다 implies dragging along the ground.

usage: 쓰레기를 쓰레기통에 던졌어요.
I threw the trash into the bin.
Destination takes 에: 쓰레기통에 던지다 = throw INTO the bin.
갑자기 질문을 던져서 당황했어요.
He suddenly threw a question at me and I was flustered.
질문을 던지다 = pose/lob a question — a set figurative phrase.
공을 멀리 던졌어요.
I threw the ball far.
멀리/세게 던지다 = throw far/hard; adverbs of distance and force pair naturally.
농담을 던지며 분위기를 풀었어요.
He cracked a joke to lighten the mood.
농담을 던지다 = toss out a joke — the 'put it out there' nuance of 던지다.
examples: 공을 던져요.
Throw the ball.
Bare command; 공을 던지다 is the core object + verb pair for throwing.
저한테 열쇠 좀 던져 주세요.
Toss me the keys, please.
Casual everyday request — 던져 주다 = throw it over to me through the air.
야구 선수가 시속 150킬로미터로 공을 던졌어요.
The baseball player pitched the ball at 150 km/h.
Real-situation use; in sports 던지다 is exactly 'to pitch/throw', here with a speed phrase.
nuance: 던지다 is the standard verb for throwing or tossing something through the air toward a spot, so the target naturally takes 에 (쓰레기통에 던지다). Its connotation is propulsion-through-air, which is why the key contrast is with 건네다 ('to hand over') and 주다 ('to give'): if you gently pass keys into someone's palm you 건네다 / 줘요, but if you lob them across the room you 던져요. Koreans extend it figuratively to 'putting something out there' — 질문을 던지다 (pose a question), 농담을 던지다 (crack a joke), 화두를 던지다 (raise a topic). A spelling point learners trip on is the past tense: 지 + 었 contracts to 졌, so it is 던졌어요, never the un-contracted '던지었어요'. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever English says 'give/pass me X' — if there is no actual flight through the air, use 주다 or 건네다, because 던지다 can sound careless or even rude with fragile or respectful objects.

The past tense contracts: write 던졌어요, not '던지었어요' (지 + 었 → 졌).
Don't drop the location particle for the target: it's 통에 던지다 ('에' = into/at), not '통을 던지다'.

usage: 휴대폰을 바닥에 떨어뜨렸어요.
I dropped my phone on the floor.
Landing spot takes 에: 바닥에 떨어뜨리다 = drop it onto the floor.
조심하세요, 컵 떨어뜨리겠어요.
Be careful, you're about to drop the cup.
-겠어요 here predicts an imminent accident the speaker foresees.
고개를 떨어뜨리고 한숨을 쉬었어요.
He dropped his head and sighed.
고개를 떨어뜨리다 = let one's head/gaze sink — a figurative, emotional use.
시험 점수를 떨어뜨리고 싶지 않아요.
I don't want to let my test score drop.
점수를 떨어뜨리다 = lower/bring down a score; the causative of 점수가 떨어지다.
examples: 컵을 떨어뜨렸어요.
I dropped the cup.
Bare statement; the object marker 을/를 is essential since this verb is causative-transitive.
계란을 떨어뜨려서 다 깨졌어요.
I dropped the eggs and they all broke.
-아서 links cause→result, pairing 떨어뜨리다 with 깨지다 ('break') for fragile things.
지하철에서 지갑을 떨어뜨린 것 같은데 어떡하죠?
I think I dropped my wallet on the subway — what should I do?
Real-situation panic; -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 ('I think I...') softens an uncertain accident.
nuance: 떨어뜨리다 is the causative/transitive partner of 떨어지다 ('to fall'): you let something fall, usually by accident, so it always takes an object and often a landing point with 에 (바닥에 떨어뜨리다). The crucial contrast is with 흘리다 and 놓치다: 흘리다 is to drop/spill things little by little without noticing (동전을 흘리다 'lose coins along the way'), and 놓치다 is to lose your grip or miss catching something (공을 놓치다 'drop/miss the ball'), whereas 떨어뜨리다 squarely means you made one specific object fall to the ground. It also works figuratively — 점수를 떨어뜨리다 (lower a score), 고개를 떨어뜨리다 (drop one's head). Morphologically it is 떨어지다 + the causative suffix -뜨리-. Because the everyday meaning is an accident, the 'please don't' form (떨어뜨리지 마세요) is what you actually hear, far more than a positive command. The English-speaker pitfall is confusing it with intransitive 떨어지다: English 'the phone dropped' and 'I dropped the phone' both use 'drop', but Korean splits them into 떨어졌어요 vs 떨어뜨렸어요.

mistakes: Don't confuse it with 떨어지다: 떨어지다 = something falls by itself (전화기가 떨어졌어요), while 떨어뜨리다 = YOU drop it (전화기를 떨어뜨렸어요).
Watch the spelling — the standard recommended form is 떨어뜨리다 (with 뜨); 떨어트리다 is also accepted but pick one and be consistent.
Don't use it for spilling/scattering things bit by bit unnoticed — that nuance is 흘리다 (동전을 흘리다), not 떨어뜨리다.

usage: 출퇴근 시간을 피해서 가세요.
Go avoiding rush hour.
N을/를 피해서 = avoiding N; the single most useful daily pattern for dodging busy times.
비를 피하려고 편의점에 들어갔어요.
I ducked into the convenience store to get out of the rain.
비를 피하다 = take shelter from rain; -(으)려고 marks the purpose.
사람을 피하지 말고 한번 이야기해 봐요.
Don't avoid the person — try talking it out.
사람을 피하다 = avoid/steer clear of someone, socially or physically.
기름진 음식을 피하세요.
Avoid greasy food.
음식을 피하다 = avoid a food/diet — common health advice.
examples: 복잡한 길을 피해서 가요.
Let's avoid the crowded street.
Simple plan; 길을 피해서 가다 = take a route that avoids it.
그 사람은 자꾸 제 눈을 피해요.
That person keeps avoiding eye contact with me.
눈을 피하다 = avoid someone's gaze — an idiom signaling guilt or discomfort.
사고를 피하려면 차간 거리를 충분히 두고 운전하세요.
To avoid an accident, drive keeping plenty of distance between cars.
Real-situation safety advice; -(으)려면 = 'if you want to avoid', stating the condition.
nuance: 피하다 means to actively avoid, dodge, or steer clear of something — a person, a situation, bad weather, or a time of day — and the workhorse construction is N을/를 피해서 ('avoiding N'), perfect for dodging rush hour (출퇴근 시간을 피해서), crowds, or the heat. It is Sino-Korean: 避(피, 'avoid/evade') + 하다, literally 'to do avoidance', which is why it can feel slightly more deliberate than a casual sidestep. The key contrast is with 빠지다 and 거르다 (to skip/miss out on something, e.g. 회의에 빠지다 'skip the meeting', 식사를 거르다 'skip a meal') and with 막다 (to block something from happening to you): 피하다 is you moving yourself out of harm's way, not blocking it. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'avoid' onto 'skip an event' — saying 회의를 피했어요 to mean 'I skipped the meeting' actually implies you dodged it on purpose, which sounds evasive; for an innocent absence use 빠지다.

It's transitive: include the thing avoided — 비를 피하다, 사람을 피하다, not bare 피하다.
Don't say '피하해요' — 하다 verbs contract to 해요, so the polite form is 피해요.

english: to turn over, to flip, to hand over
usage: 다음 장으로 넘기세요.
Turn to the next page.
페이지/장을 넘기다 = turn a page; the destination uses -(으)로 (넘어가는 방향).
이 일은 다음 주로 넘겼어요.
I pushed this task to next week.
일을/일정을 넘기다 = postpone or pass work off — make it cross over to later.
서류를 담당자에게 넘겼어요.
I handed the documents over to the person in charge.
사람에게 넘기다 = hand over / pass responsibility to someone (particle 에게/한테).
사진을 옆으로 넘기면 다음 게 나와요.
Swipe sideways and the next photo shows up.
옆으로 넘기다 = swipe to the side on a screen.
examples: 페이지를 넘겨요.
Turn the page.
Bare command; 페이지를 넘기다 is the core 'flip it over/past' meaning.
바빠서 점심을 대충 넘겼어요.
I was busy so I just got lunch over with.
Figurative 넘기다 = get past / make do with — here a meal rushed through.
힘든 시기를 가족 덕분에 잘 넘겼어요.
I got through the hard time okay thanks to my family.
Real-situation use; 시기를 넘기다 = get past a period, with 덕분에 ('thanks to') giving credit.
nuance: 넘기다 is the causative/transitive partner of 넘다 ('to cross over a line/peak'): you make something go over or past, so it spans turning pages (장을 넘기다), swiping a screen (옆으로 넘기다), handing work or objects off to someone (담당자에게 넘기다), and getting through a tough stretch of time (시기를 넘기다, 고비를 넘기다). For literally placing an object into someone's hand the sharper word is 건네다, while 넘기다 carries the extra flavor of passing something on, off, or beyond — including offloading responsibility. Watch two look-alikes: 넘다 is intransitive ('cross over' — 선을 넘다), and 넘어지다 means 'to topple/trip and fall', which has nothing to do with handing over. When the recipient is a person, mark them with 에게/한테 (담당자에게 넘기다); when it is a page or screen, mark the direction with -(으)로 (다음 장으로 넘기다). The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 넘어지다 and 넘기다 as the same root and producing '넘어겼어요' — keep them separate.

For carefully placing an object into someone's hand, 건네다 is more precise; 넘기다 stresses passing it on/off rather than the gentle handover.

usage: 무거운 상자를 혼자 들어올렸어요.
I lifted the heavy box by myself.
들어올리다 = raise something up off the ground with your hands; 혼자 ('alone') stresses the effort.
허리 다치지 않게 다리로 들어올리세요.
Lift with your legs so you don't hurt your back.
Safety phrasing; 다리로 들어올리다 = lift using your legs (수단의 -(으)로).
역도 선수가 바벨을 번쩍 들어올렸어요.
The weightlifter hoisted the barbell up in one motion.
번쩍 들어올리다 = lift in one swift heave; 번쩍 is the signature adverb.
아기를 조심해서 들어올리세요.
Lift the baby carefully.
들어올리다 of a person = pick someone up off the ground.
examples: 손을 들어올려 보세요.
Try raising your hand up.
Simple body command; -아 보세요 ('try doing') softens it into an invitation.
이 짐 좀 같이 들어올려 주실래요?
Could you help me lift this load together?
Everyday polite request for help; -아 주실래요? is a warm, soft ask.
바벨을 끝까지 들어올리지 못해서 다시 도전했어요.
I couldn't lift the barbell all the way up, so I tried again.
Real-situation gym scene; 들어올리지 못하다 = fail to lift (ability-negation 못).
nuance: 들어올리다 is a compound of 들다 ('to hold/lift in the hand') + 올리다 ('to raise'), and the whole point of the compound is to foreground the UPWARD motion — getting a heavy box, a barbell, or a child up off a surface. The contrast with plain 들다 is the dividing line learners most need: 가방을 들다 just means to hold/carry a bag (it may already be in the air), whereas 가방을 들어올리다 specifically pictures the act of heaving it up. It also differs from 올리다 alone, which can raise something already in hand (선반에 올리다 'put it up on a shelf') without the lifting-from-below nuance. Collocations cluster around weight and effort: 번쩍 들어올리다 (hoist in one motion), 끝까지 들어올리다 (lift all the way up), 다리로 들어올리다 (lift with the legs). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using it as a blanket translation of 'lift/carry' — for simply toting a bag around, 들다 is far more natural, and reserving 들어올리다 for the genuine raising action keeps your Korean from sounding heavy-handed.

english: to put down, to set down
usage: 짐을 여기에 내려놓으세요.
Put your bags down here.
Landing spot takes 에: 여기에 내려놓다 = set it down right here.
이제 그 걱정은 좀 내려놓으세요.
Now let go of that worry.
마음을/걱정을 내려놓다 = let go, ease the mind — a warm figurative use.
커피를 식탁에 살짝 내려놨어요.
I gently set the coffee on the table.
살짝 내려놓다 = set down gently; 살짝 is the natural softening adverb.
무거우면 가방을 잠깐 내려놓고 쉬어요.
If it's heavy, set the bag down for a bit and rest.
내려놓고 쉬다 = put it down and take a break — a caring suggestion.
examples: 가방을 내려놔요.
Put the bag down.
Bare casual command; note the contraction 내려놓아 → 내려놔.
무거우면 잠깐 내려놓고 쉬세요.
If it's heavy, set it down and rest a moment.
Everyday advice to someone struggling with a load.
힘든 일은 다 잊고 마음을 좀 내려놓으세요.
Forget the hard stuff and let your mind rest a little.
Real-situation comfort; the figurative 마음을 내려놓다 = release stress, like 'putting down a burden'.

Koreans use it with quiet beauty in the figurative sense 마음을 내려놓다 / 걱정을 내려놓다 — to let go of stress or attachment, exactly like the English 'put down a burden.' The English-speaker pitfall is producing '내려놔세요' by over-applying the contraction to the imperative — the polite command keeps the full stem: 내려놓으세요.

english: to flip over, to turn inside out
usage: 고기가 익으면 뒤집으세요.
Flip the meat when it's cooked.
고기를 뒤집다 = turn meat over; indispensable at the Korean BBQ grill.
빨래하기 전에 옷을 뒤집으세요.
Turn the clothes inside out before washing.
옷을 뒤집다 = turn clothing inside out — a laundry tip.
부침개를 한 번에 뒤집었어요.
I flipped the pancake in one go.
한 번에 뒤집다 = flip in a single motion; pride point when cooking 전/부침개.
그 증언이 사건을 완전히 뒤집었어요.
That testimony completely overturned the case.
Figurative 뒤집다 = overturn/upend a situation or verdict.
examples: 고기 좀 뒤집어 주세요.
Please flip the meat.
Bare polite request at the table; 뒤집어 주다 = flip it (for us).
전을 너무 일찍 뒤집으면 부서져요.
If you flip the jeon too early, it falls apart.
Everyday cooking caution; -(으)면 sets the condition, 부서지다 the bad result.
반전 소식이 분위기를 완전히 뒤집어 놨어요.
The plot-twist news totally turned the mood upside down.
Real-situation figurative use; -어 놓다 stresses the lasting upended state.
nuance: 뒤집다 means to turn something to its other side or inside out — flipping grilling meat (고기를 뒤집다), turning clothes for the wash (옷을 뒤집다), or, figuratively, overturning a situation, mood, or verdict (사건을 뒤집다). A critical conjugation warning: although the stem ends in ㅂ, this is a REGULAR verb, NOT a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ stays put — 뒤집어요, 뒤집습니다, 뒤집었어요 — and you must never soften it to '뒤지워요'. The transitivity contrast matters too: 뒤집다 is what YOU do to an object, while its passive 뒤집히다 is for something that flips or capsizes on its own (배가 뒤집혔어요 'the boat capsized'); and to knock something over face-down you might use 엎다 (그릇을 엎다 'tip the bowl over'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: assuming every ㅂ-final stem is irregular (it is not here), and using the active 뒤집다 for things that turn over by themselves when the passive 뒤집히다 is required.

english: to lean on, to rely on
usage: 벽에 기대지 마세요. 페인트 묻어요.
Don't lean on the wall, the paint comes off.
N에 기대다 = lean against a surface; the particle is 에, not 을/를.
힘들 때는 친구한테 기대도 돼요.
When it's hard, it's okay to lean on a friend.
사람한테/에게 기대다 = rely on someone emotionally; people take 한테/에게.
피곤해서 벽에 기대 잠깐 잤어요.
I was tired so I dozed leaning on the wall.
기대(서) + 다른 동작 = lean and then do something; the lean supports another action.
부모님께 너무 기대지 않으려고 해요.
I try not to rely on my parents too much.
기대지 않다 = not lean/depend on; 께 is the honorific recipient particle for 부모님.
examples: 벽에 기대요.
Lean on the wall.
Bare statement showing the core particle: 벽에 기대다, surface marked with 에.
피곤해서 창문에 기대서 잤어요.
I was so tired I slept leaning against the window.
Everyday commute scene; -아서 chains 'lean and (in that state) sleep'.
힘들 때 언제든지 나한테 기대도 돼.
Whenever it's hard, you can always lean on me.
Real-situation comfort in 반말; 기대도 돼 = 'you may lean on me', a warm offer of support.
nuance: 기대다 means to lean your body against something for physical support, and by natural extension to rely on or depend on someone emotionally. Particle choice is the heart of the word: surfaces take 에 (벽에 기대다, 창문에 기대다) and people take 에게/한테 (친구한테 기대다), or honorific 께 for elders (부모님께 기대다). The near-synonym for the figurative sense is 의지하다 ('to depend on for support'), which is a touch more serious and formal — 가족에게 의지하다 sounds weightier than the soft, warm 가족한테 기대다, and the latter still keeps the cozy image of literally leaning a shoulder. The standout English-speaker pitfall is the look-alike 기대하다 ('to expect / look forward to'): 기대돼요 means 'I'm looking forward to it' while 기대요 means 'I lean on it', and because their stems differ (기대다 vs 기대하다) mixing them up produces real confusion. Also keep the particle straight — it is 벽에 기대다, never '벽을 기대다'.

For a heavier, more formal 'depend on', 의지하다 fits better; 기대다 keeps the warm, literal 'lean a shoulder' feel.

usage: 몇 층 누르세요?
Which floor should I press?
층을 누르다 = press a floor button; the standard elevator question.
이 버튼을 길게 누르세요.
Press and hold this button.
길게 누르다 = long-press; 길게 ('lengthily') marks holding it down.
초인종을 눌렀는데 조용해요.
I rang the doorbell but it's quiet.
초인종/벨을 누르다 = ring a doorbell / press a buzzer.
좋아요 좀 눌러 주세요.
Please hit the like button.
좋아요를 누르다 = tap 'like' — everyday social-media phrasing.
examples: 버튼을 눌러요.
Press the button.
Bare command; 버튼을 누르다 is the core press-a-button pair.
엘리베이터에서 닫힘 버튼을 눌렀어요.
I pressed the close button in the elevator.
Everyday scene; note the 르-irregular past 눌렀어요 (not '누르었어요').
비밀번호를 누르고 별표를 누르면 문이 열려요.
Enter the PIN and press the star key, and the door opens.
Real-situation door-lock instructions; chained 누르고 ('press and then') sequences the steps.
nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing down — elevator buttons, doorbells, app icons, keypad keys, the 'like' button — and modern Korean life is so full of buttons that nailing it instantly sounds fluent. It is a textbook 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending, the 르 transforms and an extra ㄹ appears, so the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and past 눌렀어요, while consonant endings stay regular (누릅니다, 누르고, 누르지 마세요). The meaning contrast to lock in is with 밀다 and 당기다: 누르다 is pressing DOWN on a surface or button, 밀다 is pushing a door/object away from you (문을 밀다 'push the door'), and 당기다 is pulling it toward you (문을 당기다) — so a door says 미세요/당기세요, never 누르세요, but a doorbell beside it says 누르세요. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: writing the un-irregular '누르어요' instead of 눌러요, and over-extending 'press/push' to doors, where Korean insists on 밀다 rather than 누르다.

english: to step aside, to get out of the way
usage: 죄송한데 잠깐만 비켜 주시겠어요?
Sorry, could you step aside for a moment?
비켜 주시겠어요? = the most polite way to ask someone to move out of the way.
길 좀 비켜 주세요.
Please make way.
길을 비키다 = clear the path / get out of the way; 좀 softens the request.
뒤에서 차가 오니까 옆으로 비키세요.
A car's coming from behind, so step to the side.
옆으로 비키다 = move aside; direction marked with -(으)로.
사람들이 구급차를 위해 길을 비켰어요.
People cleared the way for the ambulance.
길을 비키다 for emergency vehicles — a civic-duty collocation.
examples: 옆으로 좀 비켜 주세요.
Please move to the side a little.
Simple polite request; 좀 + 주세요 keeps it gentle in a crowd.
뒤에서 자전거가 와서 얼른 옆으로 비켰어요.
A bike came from behind so I quickly stepped aside.
Everyday street scene; 얼른 ('quickly') captures the reflexive dodge.
문 앞을 막고 계셔서 그런데, 조금만 비켜 주시겠어요?
You're blocking the doorway, so could you move just a little?
Real-situation polite nudge; the soft preface + -주시겠어요? avoids any rudeness.
nuance: 비키다 means to step aside or move your own body out of someone's way, which makes it intransitive — you shift yourself, you do not move an object. The polite requests 비켜 주세요 and 비켜 주시겠어요? are survival phrases for crowded subways, sidewalks, and elevator doors. Register caution is essential here: a bare, curt 비켜! is genuinely rude, the equivalent of barking 'Move it!' or 'Out of my way!', so unless you intend to be sharp you must cushion it with 주세요 or the very polite 주시겠어요. The contrast to fix is with 치우다 and 옮기다, which are transitive: if a box is blocking the hall, a person 비켜요 (steps aside) but you 치워요 / 옮겨요 the box (clear/move it). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'move out of the way' as transitive and trying to 비키다 an object, or — worse — using bare 비켜 with strangers and sounding aggressive without realizing it.
